passage: Teacher's note: Arnab, Class 4. On the first day of the new term Arnab arrived in a uniform two sizes too big, with his older brother's worn black shoes. In the yard I watched him straighten his house badge and look at the other boys' shoes. When Rahul's new white sneakers were admired, Arnab put his hands behind him. At the badge ceremony, though, Gopika from his house squeezed in beside him, and Arnab stood tall and sang louder. I made a point of asking him to carry our house flag. He held it with both hands. I will keep an eye on how he feels about the shoes and talk to his parents if it keeps bothering him. 🙂

qa.q: What did Arnab straighten in the yard?
qa.a: He straightened his house badge.

qa.q: What did Arnab's hands behind his back suggest about how he felt about the sneakers, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It suggests he felt self-conscious about his old shoes. It could also just be a habit when standing in a group.

qa.q: What could the teacher do to support Arnab?
qa.a: The teacher can keep giving him roles that make him feel part of the house, watch how he feels about the shoes, and speak with his parents if the worry continues.

qa.q: How might Gopika see Arnab at the ceremony?
qa.a: Gopika, standing beside him, may see a fellow house member and simply include him. Gopika's closeness helps him feel he belongs.

grounding: A child sees a uniform and house badge signal membership, while still reading shoes as status cues.

passage: Monday night. New school, new uniform. Mine is the same as everyone's: grey trousers, white shirt, maroon tie. It felt strange but good, like being part of a team. At the gate the guard checked our ties, and I saw that Rohit's shoes were shiny and had a logo on the side. Mine are plain black and scratched. I tucked my feet under the desk in class. Then Sir said the house colours would be decided tomorrow and I got excited about being in a team. Maybe I'll be Red House. Amma polished my shoes tonight and said they looked new. I looked, and they did a bit. 🙂 — Chaitanya

qa.q: What colour tie is part of Chaitanya's uniform?
qa.a: The uniform includes a maroon tie.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya tuck both feet under the desk, and what else does the diary show Chaitanya felt about the uniform?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt self-conscious about the scratched plain shoes next to Rohit's shiny ones. The diary also shows Chaitanya felt good about the uniform, like being on a team.

qa.q: What could Chaitanya do if the shoe comparison keeps bothering Chaitanya?
qa.a: Chaitanya could talk to Amma or a teacher, and remember that the uniform makes everyone look alike apart from small things like shoes.

qa.q: How does Amma respond to Chaitanya's worry?
qa.a: Amma polishes Chaitanya's shoes and says they look new, a small, warm gesture that helps Chaitanya feel cared for.

grounding: A child notes that a uniform signals membership and reduces visible difference, yet still reads shoes as a status cue.

passage:
At the government school in the village, every child wore the same blue uniform. Hansa liked that. No one could tell who was rich.
But on Monday, Vasudha came with new white shoes, not the usual black. And a bag with shiny zips.
At lunch, a group of girls crowded round her. "Where did you get them?" Hansa looked at her own dusty chappals and tucked her feet under the bench.
Vasudha saw. "My Mama sent them from the city," she said quietly. Then she added, "Your plaits are the best in class, Hansa."
Hansa smiled a little. She still thought about the shoes all afternoon.

qa.q: What colour were Vasudha's new shoes?
qa.a: White.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she tucked her feet under the bench?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and self-conscious about her dusty chappals compared with Vasudha's new shoes.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do that helped Hansa?
qa.a: She noticed Hansa's discomfort and paid her a kind compliment about her plaits.

qa.q: How might the other girls see Vasudha's shoes?
qa.a: They saw the shoes as special and exciting, a sign of something new, even though everyone wore the same uniform.

grounding: In a village school, a child notices that uniforms reduce difference but shoes and bags still signal status.

passage:
At the primary school in Manchester, every child had a blazer with a house badge. Lars was in Green House, Camila in Red. On sports day, the houses sat in coloured rows and cheered for their own.
Lars loved his green badge. It made him feel part of a team.
But in the lunch queue he noticed something else. Camila's trainers had flashing lights, and a group of boys kept asking where she got them. Lars looked at his old trainers with the grey laces.
"The uniform's the same," he said to Camila later. "But everyone still looks at shoes."
Camila shrugged. "My cousin gave me these. They're too big." She wiggled her toes. "But yeah. People notice."

qa.q: What house was Lars in?
qa.a: Green House.

qa.q: What was Lars feeling when he looked at his old trainers?
qa.a: He felt self-conscious and a little left out, noticing that others admired Camila's flashing shoes.

qa.q: What did Lars figure out about uniforms?
qa.a: That uniforms make children look the same, but they still notice and compare shoes and other small things.

qa.q: How might Camila feel about the attention on her trainers?
qa.a: Camila seemed a bit uncomfortable, since the trainers were a hand-me-down and too big, even though others noticed them.

grounding: At a school with uniforms and house badges, a child sees belonging but also notices status cues in shoes.

passage:
At the Saturday football club in the community centre, every player got a red jersey with a number. Vandana loved hers. It made her feel part of the team.
But Disha's jersey was faded and had a tear on the shoulder, because it had been her sister's.
In the changing room, a girl said, "Why is yours so old?" Disha went red and pulled her hair over the tear.
Vandana stepped closer. "Numbers are what matter. You're number seven, the best striker."
The coach heard and said, "Same team, same jersey. What counts is how you play."
Disha smiled a little and ran onto the field first.

qa.q: What number was Disha?
qa.a: Number seven.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when she pulled her hair over the tear?
qa.a: Disha felt embarrassed and self-conscious about her old, torn jersey.

qa.q: How did Vandana and the coach help Disha?
qa.a: They reminded everyone that the jersey shows the team and how you play matters more than how new it looks.

qa.q: How might the girl who asked about the jersey see things differently after the coach spoke?
qa.a: She might realise that the team jersey is about belonging, not about having the newest one.

grounding: At a sports club, matching jerseys show membership, but children still notice and compare the condition of gear.

passage: I'm Dilnaz, and I sit behind Jagdish, who joined our school in July. On his first day he kept touching the green house badge on his pocket, as if checking it was still there. Everyone in Banyan House wears that green, so at lunch the Banyan boys waved him over, and he went. I noticed something else, though. His shoes were plain black canvas, and most of the boys had shiny leather ones with thick soles. When Arjun said, "Nice slippers," Jagdish tucked his feet under the bench and laughed along. I don't know what he was feeling. But the next day he wore the same shoes, polished very clean, and in house cricket he scored the winning run.

qa.q: What colour is the Banyan House badge?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: What might Jagdish's tucking his feet under the bench suggest?
qa.a: Possibly he felt embarrassed that his shoes marked him out, though laughing along might mean he took it lightly; Dilnaz can't be sure.

qa.q: How could a classmate help when shoes become a joke about status?
qa.a: Not laugh along, sit with Jagdish, and tell Arjun calmly that the comment wasn't kind.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz see the difference between the badge and the shoes?
qa.a: Dilnaz sees that the badge made Jagdish part of Banyan House, but the boys still read shoes as a sign of who fits, so the uniform didn't hide every difference.

grounding: It illustrates a house badge signalling membership while children still read shoes as a status cue, seen through a classmate's account.
